subject: Biology
title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
summary: The chapter explains how green plants trap light energy in the thylakoid membranes to make ATP and NADPH, and then spend those in the stroma to fix CO<sub>2</sub> into sugar by the Calvin cycle or the C<sub>4</sub> pathway. It is the base for Class 12 boards and NEET: the Z scheme, chemiosmosis, the Calvin cycle bookkeeping, Kranz anatomy, photorespiration and Blackman's law of limiting factors are asked every year in some form.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Photosynthesis in Higher Plants sits in Unit IV, Plant Physiology, which carries about 12 marks shared with Respiration in Plants and Plant Growth and Development. In a typical school final this chapter alone contributes 6 to 9 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on pigments, PAR, the first stable product or the site of a step, and an Assertion-Reason on photorespiration or cyclic photophosphorylation), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on cyclic versus non-cyclic photophosphorylation, chemiosmosis or Kranz anatomy, and very often a 5-mark question on the Z scheme, the Calvin cycle or the C<sub>4</sub> pathway with a labelled diagram. In NEET it is one of the heaviest Class 11 Botany chapters, usually two to four questions, almost all lifted from NCERT sentences and figures.

question_types.note: Metal in chlorophyll (magnesium); pigment that converts light to chemical energy (chlorophyll a); PAR 400 to 700 nm; least effective light (green); first stable product of C<sub>3</sub> (3-PGA) and C<sub>4</sub> (OAA); primary acceptor RuBP (5C) and PEP (3C); site of water splitting (inner side of thylakoid membrane, PS II); order of carriers (PS II, plastoquinone, cytochromes, PS I, ferredoxin); what cyclic photophosphorylation makes (ATP only); enzyme absent in C<sub>3</sub> plants (PEP carboxylase); light saturation at 10 per cent of full sunlight; who did which early experiment.

C<sub>4</sub> plants lack photorespiration because of the CO<sub>2</sub> concentrating mechanism; chlorophyll a is the reaction centre while accessory pigments broaden absorption; cyclic photophosphorylation occurs in stroma lamellae because they lack PS II and NADP reductase; dark reaction is not called so because it happens at night; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein; Blackman's law.

Define absorption and action spectrum; two products of light reaction used in dark reaction; write the water-splitting equation and say where it occurs; expand PAR, LHC, PGA, OAA, PEP; why the leaf kept in the dark turns yellow; what is Kranz anatomy; two conditions favouring cyclic photophosphorylation; how many ATP and NADPH per glucose.

Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation; explain chemiosmosis with the roles of F<sub>0</sub> and F<sub>1</sub>; the three stages of the Calvin cycle; why RuBisCO carboxylates more in C<sub>4</sub> plants; photorespiration and why it is wasteful; early experiments of Priestley, Ingenhousz, Engelmann or van Niel; law of limiting factors with the light-intensity graph.

Describe the Z scheme with a labelled diagram; describe the Calvin cycle with diagram and the ATP/NADPH count; describe the C<sub>4</sub> (Hatch and Slack) pathway with Kranz anatomy and list its advantages; the NCERT exercise comparison of C<sub>3</sub> versus C<sub>4</sub> pathway, cyclic versus non-cyclic photophosphorylation and leaf anatomy of C<sub>3</sub> versus C<sub>4</sub> plants; factors affecting photosynthesis.

A passage on Engelmann's prism experiment, on a greenhouse tomato farm with CO<sub>2</sub> enrichment, on a maize field versus a wheat field in summer, or on the absorption/action spectrum graph, followed by four sub-questions.

Chemiosmotic hypothesis and ATP synthase (F<sub>0</sub> and F<sub>1</sub>)
Calvin cycle: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration; 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose
C<sub>4</sub> pathway, Kranz anatomy and why C<sub>4</sub> plants are more productive
Photorespiration and the dual nature of RuBisCO
Pigments, absorption and action spectra, role of accessory pigments
Blackman's law of limiting factors and the light, CO<sub>2</sub>, temperature and water curves

sections.heading: 11.1 What do we Know?
sections.body:
Start with the definition the examiner wants. Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds. Two reasons make it the most important process on earth: it is the primary source of all food on the planet, and it is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere. Higher plants do it in the green parts, chiefly the leaves, inside the chloroplasts.

Two simple experiments from earlier classes are recalled in the chapter and can still be asked as 2-mark questions. In the variegated leaf experiment, a leaf with green and non-green patches is exposed to light and then tested for starch with iodine; only the green parts turn blue-black, proving that chlorophyll is needed. In the half-leaf experiment, part of a leaf is enclosed in a test tube containing potassium hydroxide soaked cotton (KOH absorbs CO2) while the other half stays in the air. After exposure to light, the half exposed to air tests positive for starch and the half inside the tube does not, proving that CO2 is needed. From these you already know that chlorophyll, light and CO2 are all required.

The overall equation should be written the NCERT way, with twelve water molecules on the left, because the oxygen released comes from water and not from CO2:

6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2

Read it as a redox equation: water is oxidised (it loses electrons and gives O2), and CO2 is reduced to carbohydrate. Everything that follows in the chapter is about how the light energy is captured (the light reaction) and how it is spent to reduce CO2 (the dark reaction, better called the biosynthetic phase).

formulas.expr: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 12H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + 6O<sub>2</sub> (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)
where: written on the left so that all six O<sub>2</sub> come from water, not from CO<sub>2</sub>

sections.tip: If asked to write the equation, use 12H<sub>2</sub>O on the left and 6H<sub>2</sub>O on the right. The simplified 6H<sub>2</sub>O version is accepted in lower classes, but at this level the examiner expects you to show that oxygen comes from water.

sections.heading: 11.2 Early Experiments
sections.body:
The chapter lists five scientists and the examiner expects you to match each name to its finding. Learn them as a story.

Joseph Priestley (1770) placed a burning candle in a closed bell jar; it went out. A mouse in a closed jar suffocated. When he put a mint plant in the jar with the candle or the mouse, the candle kept burning and the mouse stayed alive. He concluded that plants restore to the air whatever the burning candle or the breathing animal removes; he had found that plants release oxygen (he called the air 'dephlogisticated').

Jan Ingenhousz (1730 to 1799) repeated the experiment in light and in dark and showed that sunlight is essential to the process. Using an aquatic plant he saw that in bright sunlight small bubbles (oxygen) formed around the green parts, and in dark no bubbles formed. So only the green parts of the plant release oxygen, and only in light.

Julius von Sachs (1854) provided evidence that plants produce glucose when they grow and that it is usually stored as starch. He also showed that the green substance (chlorophyll) is located in special bodies in the cell, later called chloroplasts.

T. W. Engelmann (1843 to 1909) split light with a prism into its colours, illuminated a filament of the green alga Cladophora placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria, and watched where the bacteria gathered. They accumulated mainly in the blue and red regions of the spectrum, where the most oxygen was being released. This gave the first action spectrum of photosynthesis, which matches the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a and b.

Cornelius van Niel (1897 to 1985) worked with purple and green sulphur bacteria, which use H2S instead of water and release sulphur, not oxygen. From this he proposed that photosynthesis is essentially a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO2 to carbohydrate, and that in green plants the hydrogen donor is water, so the O2 released comes from water, not from CO2. This was later proved using radioisotopes.

formulas.expr: 2H<sub>2</sub>A + CO<sub>2</sub> → 2A + CH<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O (van Niel's general equation)
where: the hydrogen donor: H<sub>2</sub>S in sulphur bacteria, H<sub>2</sub>O in green plants

formulas.expr: Purple and green sulphur bacteria: CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>S → CH<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O + 2S
where: sulphur is released, no oxygen; proof that O<sub>2</sub> in plants comes from H<sub>2</sub>O

sections.tip: Engelmann used a prism, Cladophora and aerobic bacteria; van Niel used sulphur bacteria. Students mix these two. Also note that Priestley found oxygen release but Ingenhousz showed the need for light and green parts.

sections.heading: 11.3 Where does Photosynthesis take place?
sections.body:
Photosynthesis takes place in the green parts of the plant, mainly in the mesophyll cells of the leaf, which have a large number of chloroplasts. Inside the mesophyll cell the chloroplasts align themselves along the cell walls so that they receive the optimum amount of incident light.

The structure to draw and label is NCERT Figure 11.1. A chloroplast has a double membrane envelope enclosing two compartments: the membranous system made of grana (stacks of thylakoids), the stroma lamellae that connect the grana, and the fluid stroma in which the membranes are embedded. Also mark the thylakoid lumen, the space inside a thylakoid, because it matters for chemiosmosis later.

The division of labour is a standard 2-mark answer. The membrane system (grana and stroma lamellae) is responsible for trapping light energy and for the synthesis of ATP and NADPH. That is the light reaction. In the stroma the enzymatic reactions take place that incorporate CO2 into the plant to make sugar, which in turn forms starch. Those are the dark reactions. The name is a trap: the dark reactions do not require light directly, but they depend on the ATP and NADPH made by the light reaction, so in practice they run in daylight. NCERT points out that calling them dark reactions is misleading, and the better term is biosynthetic phase or carbon reactions.

Keep the two-compartment picture in mind for the whole chapter. Every light-driven step (water splitting, electron flow, proton pumping, ATP synthase) is a membrane event; every carbon-fixing step (RuBisCO, PEP carboxylase in mesophyll of C4 plants, the Calvin cycle) is a stroma event.

formulas.expr: Membrane system (grana + stroma lamellae): light trapping, ATP and NADPH synthesis = light reaction
where: stacks of thylakoids, carry PS I and PS II
unstacked membranes joining grana; carry PS I only

formulas.expr: Stroma: CO<sub>2</sub> fixation and sugar synthesis = dark reaction (biosynthetic phase)
where: fluid matrix containing RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle enzymes

sections.tip: If asked 'why are the dark reactions called so, and is the name correct', answer that they do not directly depend on light but they do depend on the products of the light reaction, so they cannot go on for long in the dark.

sections.heading: 11.4 How many Types of Pigments are involved in Photosynthesis?
sections.body:
Leaves look green because of a mixture of pigments, not one. Separate a leaf extract by paper chromatography and four bands appear: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green in the chromatogram), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). Pigments are substances that absorb specific wavelengths of light; the colour we see is what is not absorbed.

Two graphs are asked together (NCERT Figure 11.4). The absorption spectrum of a pigment is a plot of the amount of light absorbed against wavelength. The action spectrum of photosynthesis is a plot of the rate of photosynthesis (measured, for example, as O2 evolved) against wavelength. Chlorophyll a shows peaks in the blue and the red regions and a trough in the green. The action spectrum has the same shape, with maximum photosynthesis in blue and red and least in green. Because the action spectrum overlaps the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a so closely, chlorophyll a is the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis. The overlap is not perfect, and the small gap shows that other pigments also contribute.

Why keep chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids at all? These are accessory pigments. They absorb light at wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a, so the plant uses a wider band of the incident light. They also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation. That is the answer to NCERT exercise 5: a plant with chlorophyll b but no chlorophyll a would not photosynthesise, because only chlorophyll a at the reaction centre converts light energy into chemical energy; the accessory pigments can only hand energy over.

The band of wavelengths usable by plants, roughly 400 to 700 nm, is called photosynthetically active radiation (PAR). Green light (around 500 to 550 nm) is the least effective colour because it is largely reflected.

formulas.expr: Chromatogram bands: chlorophyll a (bright/blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange)
where: chief pigment; the only one that converts light energy to chemical energy at the reaction centre

formulas.expr: Absorption spectrum = light absorbed vs wavelength; action spectrum = rate of photosynthesis vs wavelength; peaks in blue and red, minimum in green

sections.tip: Two-line answer to 'why do plants have accessory pigments': (1) they absorb wavelengths chlorophyll a cannot and pass the energy to it, widening the range of usable light; (2) they protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation. Both points are marked.

sections.heading: 11.5 What is Light Reaction?
sections.body:
The light reaction, also called the photochemical phase, includes four events: light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release, and the formation of ATP and NADPH. All four happen on the thylakoid membranes.

The pigments are not scattered; they are organised into two discrete photosystems, Photosystem I (PS I) and Photosystem II (PS II), named in the order in which they were discovered, not the order in which they act. Each photosystem is a light harvesting complex (LHC) made of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins. In each, a single chlorophyll a molecule forms the reaction centre, and all the other pigments (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids) form the antenna, whose job is to absorb light of different wavelengths and funnel the energy to the reaction centre.

The two reaction centres differ in the wavelength at which their chlorophyll a absorbs best. In PS I the reaction centre chlorophyll a has its absorption peak at 700 nm and is called P700. In PS II the peak is at 680 nm and it is called P680. Draw NCERT Figure 11.5 when asked about the LHC: a fan of pigment molecules pointing inward to one reaction-centre chlorophyll a, with arrows showing energy transfer.

Why two photosystems? The energy needed to lift an electron all the way from water (a poor electron donor) to NADP+ (making the strong reductant NADPH) is more than one photon at a single centre can provide. So the electron is boosted twice, once at PS II and once at PS I. That is the logic of the Z scheme in the next section.

formulas.expr: Light reaction = light absorption + water splitting + O<sub>2</sub> release + ATP and NADPH formation
PS I reaction centre = P700; PS II reaction centre = P680; each is a single chlorophyll a surrounded by antenna pigments
where: light harvesting complex of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins

sections.tip: PS I and PS II are numbered by order of discovery, so in the electron pathway PS II acts first. Examiners like the MCQ 'which photosystem is excited first', and the answer is PS II.

sections.heading: 11.6 The Electron Transport (Z scheme)
sections.body:
This is the diagram most often asked for 5 marks, NCERT Figure 11.6. Learn it as a sequence of six steps and draw it as a Z lying on its side, with redox potential on the vertical axis.

Step 1. In PS II the reaction centre chlorophyll a (P680) absorbs 680 nm red light and becomes excited. It gives up an electron to a primary electron acceptor, which now has a higher energy than the electron had in P680.

Step 2. The electron passes from the primary acceptor to an electron transport system (ETS) made of cytochromes. The electron moves downhill in terms of redox potential, and as it passes through the chain some of its energy is used to make ATP (see chemiosmosis, 11.6.3). The exemplar order of carriers is PS II, plastoquinone, cytochromes, PS I, ferredoxin.

Step 3. The electron reaches the pigments of PS I, filling the hole left when P700 loses its electron. In this way PS II continuously supplies electrons to PS I.

Step 4. P700 in PS I absorbs red light (700 nm), becomes excited, and passes an electron to another acceptor that has a higher redox potential.

Step 5. From this acceptor the electron again moves downhill, through ferredoxin, to NADP+. The enzyme NADP reductase on the stroma side adds two electrons and a proton to reduce NADP+ to NADPH + H+.

Step 6. PS II is left short of an electron. That hole is filled by electrons from water, which is split to give protons, electrons and O2 (section 11.6.1).

This whole scheme of transfer of electrons, starting from PS II, uphill to the acceptor, downhill to PS I, excitation of electrons, transfer to another acceptor, and finally downhill to NADP+, is called the Z scheme, because of its shape when the carriers are placed on a redox-potential scale. The net products of one pass are ATP, NADPH and O2. Because electrons flow in one direction from water to NADP+ and do not return, this is non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

formulas.expr: H<sub>2</sub>O → PS II (P680) → primary acceptor → plastoquinone → cytochromes (ATP formed) → PS I (P700) → acceptor → ferredoxin → NADP reductase → NADPH + H<sup>+</sup>
where: reaction-centre chlorophyll a of PS II and PS I
enzyme on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane

formulas.expr: Products of non-cyclic electron flow: ATP + NADPH + O<sub>2</sub>
where: released from water splitting, not from CO<sub>2</sub>

sections.tip: In the Z scheme diagram, the two uphill arrows are the two photon absorptions and both downhill runs are 'spontaneous'. Label P680, P700, the two primary acceptors, the cytochrome chain with 'ATP' beside it, ferredoxin, NADP<sup>+</sup> → NADPH and water splitting at the bottom left. Five labels correctly placed are what the marking scheme looks for.

sections.heading: 11.6.1 Splitting of Water
sections.body:
P680, having lost its electron, must get one back or PS II stops. The electrons come from water. The water-splitting complex is associated with PS II, which itself is physically located on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, facing the lumen. Water is split into protons (H+), electrons (e−) and oxygen (O2). Write it as:

2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−

Three consequences are examined. First, the electrons replace those that PS II lost, so P680 is regenerated and the Z scheme keeps running. Second, the oxygen is a by-product that diffuses out; this is the source of atmospheric oxygen and the confirmation of van Niel's proposal that O2 comes from water, not CO2. Third, the protons are released inside the thylakoid lumen, which is one of the ways the proton gradient of chemiosmosis is built (section 11.6.3).

The splitting of water is also called photolysis of water, because light energy absorbed by PS II drives it. Manganese, calcium and chloride ions are associated with the water-splitting complex; NCERT does not go into the details, so a mention is enough. What NCERT does stress, and what MCQs test, is the location: water is split on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, by the complex linked to PS II, and the O2 released has its source in H2O.

formulas.expr: 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 4H<sup>+</sup> + O<sub>2</sub> + 4e<sup>−</sup>
where: inner side of the thylakoid membrane, water-splitting complex associated with PS II
replace the electrons lost by P680
accumulate in the thylakoid lumen and help build the proton gradient

sections.tip: The exemplar MCQ 'splitting of water is associated with' has the answer 'inner surface of the thylakoid membrane', not 'lumen of thylakoid' or 'PS I'. Know both the photosystem (PS II) and the surface (inner).

sections.heading: 11.6.2 Cyclic and Non-cyclic Photo-phosphorylation
sections.body:
Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light, by living cells (chloroplasts). It is the light-driven counterpart of oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. There are two forms, and the comparison is one of the most regular 3-mark and 5-mark questions.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation. Both PS II and PS I work in series. Electrons flow from water through PS II, the cytochrome chain, PS I and ferredoxin to NADP+, and do not return. Products: ATP and NADPH, with O2 released from water. Site: the grana lamellae, whose membranes carry both photosystems.

Cyclic photophosphorylation. Only PS I is involved. The electron excited from P700 is passed to the acceptor but, instead of going to NADP+, is circulated back to the PS I complex through the electron transport chain. The cyclic flow makes only ATP; no NADPH is formed and no O2 is released because water is not split. It possibly occurs in the stroma lamellae, since these membranes lack PS II and NADP reductase and therefore cannot run the non-cyclic route. Cyclic flow also takes over when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available, because such light excites P700 but not P680.

Why does the plant need a cyclic route at all? The Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP for every 2 NADPH, but non-cyclic flow makes roughly equal amounts. Cyclic photophosphorylation tops up the ATP without making extra NADPH.

For the tabular comparison, use these rows: photosystems involved (PS I and PS II versus PS I only), electron pathway (non-cyclic, from water to NADP+ versus cyclic, back to PS I), water splitting and O2 evolution (yes versus no), products (ATP and NADPH versus ATP only), site (grana versus stroma lamellae), and light condition (both 680 and 700 nm versus beyond 680 nm).

formulas.expr: Non-cyclic: PS II + PS I; H<sub>2</sub>O split; products ATP + NADPH + O<sub>2</sub>; site grana lamellae
where: carry both PS I and PS II

formulas.expr: Cyclic: PS I only; electron returns to P700; product ATP only; no O<sub>2</sub>; site stroma lamellae; occurs when light is beyond 680 nm
where: lack PS II and NADP reductase

sections.tip: The exemplar asks you to complete a flowchart for cyclic photophosphorylation: PS I (P700) → electron acceptor → electron transport chain → back to PS I, with ATP formed along the chain. Draw exactly that and write 'only ATP formed' beside it.

sections.heading: 11.6.3 Chemiosmotic Hypothesis
sections.body:
How does electron flow make ATP? The answer is chemiosmosis, proposed by Peter Mitchell and used in both chloroplasts and mitochondria. ATP synthesis is linked to the development of a proton gradient across a membrane. In the chloroplast the protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen, while in mitochondria they accumulate in the intermembrane space. The gradient forms in three ways, each a marking point.

(1) Splitting of water takes place on the inner side of the membrane, so the protons it produces accumulate in the lumen.

(2) The primary electron acceptor of PS II, located towards the outer (stroma) side of the membrane, hands its electron not to an electron carrier but to an H carrier (plastoquinone). This molecule picks up a proton from the stroma as it takes the electron; when it passes the electron to the next carrier on the inner side of the membrane, it releases the proton into the lumen. So protons are pumped from stroma to lumen.

(3) NADP reductase sits on the stroma side of the membrane. The protons needed to reduce NADP+ to NADPH + H+ are taken from the stroma, lowering the proton concentration there further.

The result is a decrease of protons in the stroma and an accumulation in the lumen: a proton gradient and a pH difference across the thylakoid membrane. The gradient is broken down by movement of protons across the membrane through the transmembrane channel of the enzyme ATP synthase (ATPase). This enzyme has two parts. F0 is embedded in the membrane and forms the channel that carries out facilitated diffusion of protons across it. F1 protrudes on the outer surface of the membrane, on the side facing the stroma. The breakdown of the gradient releases enough energy to cause a conformational change in F1, which makes the enzyme synthesise ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

Summarise the whole light reaction in one sentence: it needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase, and its products, ATP and NADPH, are used in the stroma to fix CO2.

formulas.expr: Proton gradient built by (1) water splitting in the lumen, (2) H carrier pumping H<sup>+</sup> from stroma into lumen, (3) NADP reductase removing H<sup>+</sup> from the stroma
ADP + Pi → ATP, driven by H<sup>+</sup> diffusing through F<sub>0</sub> and a conformational change in F<sub>1</sub> of ATP synthase
where: transmembrane proton channel, embedded in the thylakoid membrane
catalytic head protruding into the stroma

sections.tip: The classic error is to say protons accumulate in the stroma. They accumulate in the thylakoid lumen; the stroma loses protons. Also note that in chloroplasts F<sub>1</sub> faces the stroma, in mitochondria F<sub>1</sub> faces the matrix.

sections.heading: 11.7 Where are the ATP and NADPH Used? and 11.7.1 The Primary Acceptor of CO2
sections.body:
The products of the light reaction, ATP, NADPH and O2, have different fates. O2 diffuses out of the chloroplast. ATP and NADPH are used in the stroma to drive the processes that reduce CO2 to sugars. This is the biosynthetic phase. It does not directly depend on light, but it depends on the products of the light reaction. If light stops, the biosynthetic phase continues for a short while and then stops; if light is restored, it restarts. That is the correct answer to 'is the term dark reaction justified'.

Historically, CO2 fixation was traced by Melvin Calvin and co-workers using the radioactive isotope 14C in algal photosynthesis. They found that the first stable CO2 fixation product is a 3-carbon organic acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA). Plants in which this is the first product are called C3 plants, and the pathway is the C3 pathway or Calvin cycle. Later, in some plants, the first stable product was found to be a 4-carbon organic acid, oxaloacetic acid (OAA); these are C4 plants.

The primary acceptor of CO2 was a puzzle for a while because scientists expected a 2-carbon acceptor (2C + CO2 = 3C). It turned out to be a 5-carbon ketose sugar, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP). RuBP + CO2 gives an unstable 6-carbon compound that immediately splits into two molecules of 3-PGA. In C4 plants the primary acceptor in the mesophyll is the 3-carbon phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), giving the 4-carbon OAA.

One line to remember: the Calvin cycle occurs in all photosynthetic plants, whether they have the C3 or the C4 pathway. The C4 route is an addition in front of the Calvin cycle, not a replacement.

formulas.expr: RuBP (5C) + CO<sub>2</sub> → unstable 6C intermediate → 2 × 3-PGA (3C), catalysed by RuBisCO
where: ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor of C<sub>3</sub> plants

formulas.expr: PEP (3C) + CO<sub>2</sub> → OAA (4C), catalysed by PEP carboxylase in mesophyll of C<sub>4</sub> plants
where: phosphoenol pyruvate, primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor of C<sub>4</sub> plants

sections.tip: Two MCQ pairs: primary acceptor (RuBP in C<sub>3</sub>, PEP in C<sub>4</sub>) and first stable product (3-PGA in C<sub>3</sub>, OAA in C<sub>4</sub>). 'Primary CO<sub>2</sub> fixation' is catalysed by both RuBP carboxylase and PEP carboxylase, depending on the plant.

sections.heading: 11.7.2 The Calvin Cycle
sections.body:
The Calvin cycle was worked out by Calvin, Benson and Bassham. It runs in the stroma of every photosynthetic plant and has three stages: carboxylation, reduction and regeneration. Draw it as a circle (NCERT Figure 11.8) with CO2 entering at the top, RuBP and 3-PGA on the ring, ATP and NADPH consumed on the reduction arm, ATP consumed on the regeneration arm, and sucrose (or triose phosphate) leaving.

Carboxylation. CO2 is fixed into a stable organic intermediate. RuBP (5C) accepts CO2 to give two molecules of 3-PGA. The enzyme is RuBP carboxylase, called RuBisCO because it also has an oxygenase activity (section 11.8). This is the most crucial step of the cycle.

Reduction. A series of reactions that lead to the formation of glucose. This stage uses 2 ATP for phosphorylation and 2 NADPH for reduction per CO2 molecule fixed. The fixation of six CO2 molecules and six turns of the cycle are needed to remove one molecule of glucose from the pathway.

Regeneration. RuBP, the CO2 acceptor, must be regenerated for the cycle to continue. This needs 1 ATP per CO2 for the phosphorylation that forms RuBP.

Now the bookkeeping that the 3-mark question tests. Per CO2: 2 ATP + 1 ATP = 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. For one glucose (6 CO2, six turns): 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. NCERT states it as a balance sheet: In: 6 CO2, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH. Out: 1 glucose, 18 ADP, 12 NADP+. The ATP and NADPH are supplied by the light reaction, which is why the Calvin cycle cannot run for long in the dark.

Two connections make good answers. Six turns are needed because each turn fixes only one carbon and glucose has six. And the mismatch between 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2 explains why plants need cyclic photophosphorylation in addition to the non-cyclic route.

formulas.expr: Per CO<sub>2</sub> fixed: carboxylation (RuBisCO, 0 ATP) → reduction (2 ATP + 2 NADPH) → regeneration of RuBP (1 ATP); total 3 ATP + 2 NADPH
where: 3-PGA is phosphorylated and reduced to triose phosphate
RuBP re-formed so the cycle continues

formulas.expr: Per glucose: 6 CO<sub>2</sub> + 18 ATP + 12 NADPH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 18 ADP + 12 NADP<sup>+</sup> (six turns of the cycle)
where: one CO<sub>2</sub> enters per turn; glucose has six carbons

sections.tip: Write the three stage names in order and attach the ATP/NADPH cost to the right stage. Students often put NADPH in regeneration; it is used only in reduction.

sections.heading: 11.7.3 The C4 Pathway
sections.body:
C4 plants, mostly tropical grasses such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane, have oxaloacetic acid as the first CO2 fixation product. They share four features that make them examination favourites: they have a special leaf anatomy, they tolerate higher temperatures, they respond to high light intensities, they lack photorespiration, and they have greater productivity of biomass.

Kranz anatomy. In a C4 leaf the vascular bundles are surrounded by a ring of particularly large cells called bundle sheath cells; 'Kranz' means wreath, describing this arrangement. The bundle sheath cells may form several layers around the bundle. They have a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange, and no intercellular spaces. C3 leaves show no such sheath and the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy layers. Looking at a plant from outside you cannot tell C3 from C4; a transverse section of the leaf can.

The Hatch and Slack pathway (NCERT Figure 11.10) needs both cell types. In the mesophyll cells, the primary acceptor PEP (3C) fixes CO2 to form OAA (4C), catalysed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase). Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO. OAA is converted to other 4-carbon acids such as malic acid or aspartic acid, which are transported to the bundle sheath cells. There the C4 acid is decarboxylated, releasing CO2 and a 3-carbon molecule (pyruvate). The bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase, so the released CO2 enters the Calvin cycle and sugar is made there. The 3-carbon molecule is transported back to the mesophyll, where it is converted to PEP again (this costs ATP), completing the cycle.

The purpose of all this is to be a CO2 concentrating mechanism. By pumping carbon into the bundle sheath and releasing it there, the plant builds a high CO2 concentration around RuBisCO, which keeps the enzyme working as a carboxylase and suppresses its oxygenase activity. That is why only a few cells (bundle sheath) run the Calvin cycle yet the plant is highly productive: those cells are never starved of CO2, never lose fixed carbon to photorespiration, and the whole leaf feeds them.

formulas.expr: Mesophyll: PEP (3C) + CO<sub>2</sub> → OAA (4C) via PEP carboxylase → malate/aspartate → bundle sheath: decarboxylation → CO<sub>2</sub> (to Calvin cycle via RuBisCO) + pyruvate (3C) → back to mesophyll → PEP regenerated (ATP used)
where: has RuBisCO, lacks PEPcase; runs the Calvin cycle

formulas.expr: Kranz anatomy: bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gases, no intercellular spaces

sections.tip: For the 5-mark question, give the diagram with both cells drawn side by side and the four molecules (PEP, OAA, C<sub>4</sub> acid, pyruvate) placed correctly, then a separate list of advantages: high temperature tolerance, high light response, no photorespiration, higher biomass, functions with stomata partly closed.

sections.heading: 11.8 Photorespiration
sections.body:
RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme in the world, and it has an odd feature: its active site can bind both CO2 and O2, which compete for it. The enzyme has a much greater affinity for CO2 than for O2, so which reaction wins depends on the relative concentration of the two gases at the enzyme.

In C3 plants, on a hot bright day the stomata partly close, CO2 inside the leaf falls and O2 (a product of the light reaction) rises. Some O2 now binds RuBisCO, and RuBP, instead of being carboxylated to two molecules of 3-PGA, is oxygenated to one molecule of phosphoglycerate (3C) and one molecule of phosphoglycolate (2C). This is photorespiration, a light-dependent, oxygen-consuming process. In the photorespiratory pathway there is no synthesis of sugars, no ATP and no NADPH; instead it results in the release of CO2 with the utilisation of ATP. So it is a wasteful process that undoes part of the Calvin cycle's work. It involves the chloroplast, the peroxisome and the mitochondrion.

In C4 plants photorespiration does not occur. They have the CO2 concentrating mechanism of the Hatch and Slack pathway: C4 acids made in the mesophyll are broken down in the bundle sheath cells, releasing CO2 right where RuBisCO is, so the intracellular CO2 concentration is high and the enzyme functions as a carboxylase, with oxygenase activity minimised. That is the full answer to NCERT exercise 4 (why RuBisCO carries out more carboxylation in C4 plants) and to exemplar's 'why is photorespiration absent in C4 plants'.

The consequence is a difference in productivity and tolerance. C4 plants show high productivity, tolerate high temperatures, and can keep photosynthesising with partly closed stomata; C3 plants lose up to a quarter of the carbon they fix on hot days to photorespiration. The exemplar also asks under what conditions C4 plants are superior: high temperature, high light intensity and low CO2 or water stress, precisely the conditions that favour the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO in C3 plants.

formulas.expr: Carboxylation: RuBP + CO<sub>2</sub> → 2 × 3-PGA (3C); Oxygenation: RuBP + O<sub>2</sub> → 1 phosphoglycerate (3C) + 1 phosphoglycolate (2C)
where: ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase; affinity for CO<sub>2</sub> much higher than for O<sub>2</sub>
the 2C product that starts the photorespiratory pathway

formulas.expr: Photorespiration: no sugar, no ATP, no NADPH; CO<sub>2</sub> released with ATP used; absent in C<sub>4</sub> plants
where: CO<sub>2</sub> concentrating mechanism keeps RuBisCO in carboxylase mode

sections.tip: Do not call photorespiration a form of respiration that yields energy. Its defining points are: light-dependent, uses O<sub>2</sub>, releases CO<sub>2</sub>, consumes ATP, produces neither sugar nor ATP nor NADPH.

sections.heading: 11.9 Factors affecting Photosynthesis: light, CO2, temperature and water
sections.body:
The rate of photosynthesis depends on both plant factors (number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO2 concentration and chlorophyll content) and external factors (sunlight, temperature, CO2 and water). Because these act together, the chapter states Blackman's (1905) Law of Limiting Factors: if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, then its rate will be determined by the factor which is nearest to its minimal value; it is the factor which directly affects the process if its quantity is changed. Learn this sentence; it is quoted verbatim in answers. Example: with plenty of light, CO2 and chlorophyll but low temperature, the rate is set by temperature; raise the temperature and the rate rises until some other factor becomes limiting.

Light. Consider light quality, intensity and duration. At low intensities there is a linear relationship between incident light and CO2 fixation. At higher intensities the rate does not keep rising, because other factors become limiting. Light saturation occurs at about 10 per cent of full sunlight, so except for plants in shade or in dense forests light is rarely a limiting factor in nature. Very high light causes breakdown of chlorophyll and a fall in the rate. NCERT Figure 11.11 shows the curve; in the rising region (A) light is limiting, at the plateau (C, D) some other factor is.

Carbon dioxide. CO2 is the major limiting factor. Its concentration in the atmosphere is very low, between 0.03 and 0.04 per cent; raising it up to 0.05 per cent increases CO2 fixation, but beyond that it is damaging over long periods. C3 and C4 plants respond differently. At low light both respond little; at high light both respond to higher CO2. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µl L−1, while C3 plants keep responding and saturate only beyond 450 µl L−1, so present-day atmospheric CO2 is limiting for C3 plants. This is used in greenhouses: crops such as tomatoes and bell pepper are grown in CO2-enriched air to raise yield.

Temperature. The dark reactions are enzymatic and therefore temperature controlled; light reactions are also temperature sensitive but to a much lesser extent. C4 plants respond to higher temperatures and show a higher rate, while C3 plants have a much lower temperature optimum. Tropical plants have a higher optimum than temperate plants, because plants adapt to their habitat.

Water. Water is a raw material, but its effect is felt more through the plant than through the reaction. Water stress closes the stomata, reducing CO2 availability, and makes leaves wilt, reducing their surface area and metabolic activity.

formulas.expr: Blackman's law (1905): the rate of a process affected by several factors is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value
where: the factor whose change directly alters the rate

formulas.expr: Light: linear at low intensity; saturation at about 10 per cent of full sunlight
where: beyond this light is no longer limiting; other factors are

formulas.expr: CO<sub>2</sub>: atmospheric 0.03 to 0.04 per cent; C<sub>4</sub> saturates at about 360 µl L<sup>−1</sup>, C<sub>3</sub> beyond 450 µl L<sup>−1</sup>
where: tomatoes, bell pepper grown in CO<sub>2</sub>-enriched air

sections.tip: For the light-intensity graph, write three things: in the linear part light is limiting; at the plateau CO<sub>2</sub> (or temperature) is limiting; the plateau itself is the light-saturation point. Naming a plausible limiting factor for the plateau earns the mark.

key_terms.definition: A physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds (sugars) from CO<sub>2</sub> and water, releasing O<sub>2</sub>. It is the primary source of all food on earth.
A graph of the amount of light absorbed by a pigment against wavelength. Chlorophyll a absorbs maximally in the blue and red regions.

A graph of the rate of photosynthesis (for example O<sub>2</sub> evolved) against the wavelength of light. It overlaps the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a, showing that chlorophyll a is the chief pigment.
Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids. They absorb wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and transfer the energy to it, and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
The band of wavelengths, about 400 to 700 nm, that plants can use for photosynthesis.
A photosystem's assembly of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins; the antenna pigments absorb light and funnel energy to the single chlorophyll a reaction centre.
The single chlorophyll a molecule in a photosystem that converts light energy into chemical energy by losing an excited electron: P700 in PS I, P680 in PS II.

The scheme of electron transfer from PS II uphill to a primary acceptor, downhill through cytochromes to PS I, uphill again to another acceptor and downhill to NADP<sup>+</sup>, so named because of its Z shape on a redox-potential scale.

The light-driven splitting of water, 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 4H<sup>+</sup> + O<sub>2</sub> + 4e<sup>−</sup>, by the water-splitting complex associated with PS II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane.
Synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light in chloroplasts. Non-cyclic (PS I and PS II, gives ATP and NADPH) or cyclic (PS I only, gives ATP only).

The mechanism by which ATP is synthesised using a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane; protons accumulate in the lumen and flow back through F<sub>0</sub> of ATP synthase, causing a conformational change in F<sub>1</sub> that makes ATP.

Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase, the enzyme that fixes CO<sub>2</sub> onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle; it can also bind O<sub>2</sub>, causing photorespiration. The most abundant enzyme in the world.
The stroma pathway of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation in which RuBP accepts CO<sub>2</sub> to give 3-PGA; three stages, carboxylation, reduction and regeneration; 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.

A CO<sub>2</sub> concentrating pathway in which PEP fixes CO<sub>2</sub> to OAA in mesophyll cells and the C<sub>4</sub> acid is decarboxylated in bundle sheath cells to feed CO<sub>2</sub> to the Calvin cycle.
The leaf anatomy of C<sub>4</sub> plants in which large bundle sheath cells, with many chloroplasts, thick gas-impervious walls and no intercellular spaces, form a wreath around the vascular bundles.

The light-dependent process in C<sub>3</sub> plants in which RuBisCO binds O<sub>2</sub> instead of CO<sub>2</sub>, forming phosphoglycolate; it releases CO<sub>2</sub>, uses ATP and makes no sugar, ATP or NADPH.
Blackman's 1905 law: when a process is affected by several factors, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value.

formula_sheet.note: 12 water on the left so that all O<sub>2</sub> comes from water; water oxidised, CO<sub>2</sub> reduced.

formula_sheet.name: Early experiments

formula_sheet.note: Match name to finding; MCQ and 2-mark favourite.

formula_sheet.name: Chloroplast division of labour
formula_sheet.expr: Grana + stroma lamellae: light reaction (ATP, NADPH); stroma: dark reaction (CO<sub>2</sub> fixation to sugar and starch)
formula_sheet.note: Stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase, so only cyclic photophosphorylation there.

formula_sheet.name: Pigments in the chromatogram
formula_sheet.expr: Chlorophyll a bright/blue-green; chlorophyll b yellow-green; xanthophylls yellow; carotenoids yellow to yellow-orange; PAR 400 to 700 nm; green light least effective; Mg in chlorophyll
formula_sheet.note: Chlorophyll a is the only pigment that converts light to chemical energy; others are accessory.

formula_sheet.name: Photosystems
formula_sheet.expr: PS I reaction centre P700; PS II reaction centre P680; each LHC = antenna pigments + one chlorophyll a reaction centre; PS II acts first in the Z scheme
formula_sheet.note: Numbered by order of discovery, not order of action.

formula_sheet.name: Water splitting
formula_sheet.expr: 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 4H<sup>+</sup> + O<sub>2</sub> + 4e<sup>−</sup>; complex associated with PS II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane
formula_sheet.note: Electrons replace those lost by P680; protons go into the lumen.

formula_sheet.name: Cyclic vs non-cyclic photophosphorylation
formula_sheet.expr: Non-cyclic: PS II + PS I, water split, ATP + NADPH + O<sub>2</sub>, grana. Cyclic: PS I only, electron returns to P700, ATP only, no O<sub>2</sub>, stroma lamellae, light beyond 680 nm

formula_sheet.name: Chemiosmosis
formula_sheet.expr: Proton gradient (lumen high H<sup>+</sup>) from water splitting, H carrier pumping and NADP reductase; ATP synthase F<sub>0</sub> (membrane channel) + F<sub>1</sub> (stroma-facing head, conformational change) makes ATP
formula_sheet.note: Protons accumulate in the lumen, not the stroma.

formula_sheet.name: Calvin cycle bookkeeping
formula_sheet.expr: Per CO<sub>2</sub>: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH (reduction 2 ATP + 2 NADPH, regeneration 1 ATP). Per glucose (6 turns): 18 ATP + 12 NADPH
formula_sheet.note: Stages: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration. Acceptor RuBP (5C); first product 3-PGA (3C).

formula_sheet.name: C<sub>4</sub> pathway
formula_sheet.expr: Mesophyll: PEP + CO<sub>2</sub> → OAA (PEPcase; no RuBisCO). Bundle sheath: C<sub>4</sub> acid → CO<sub>2</sub> + pyruvate; CO<sub>2</sub> into Calvin cycle (RuBisCO). Pyruvate back to mesophyll → PEP
formula_sheet.note: Examples maize, sorghum, sugarcane; Kranz anatomy; no photorespiration; higher biomass.

formula_sheet.name: Photorespiration
formula_sheet.expr: RuBP + O<sub>2</sub> → phosphoglycerate (3C) + phosphoglycolate (2C); releases CO<sub>2</sub>, uses ATP, no sugar/ATP/NADPH; absent in C<sub>4</sub> plants
formula_sheet.note: Favoured by high O<sub>2</sub>, low CO<sub>2</sub>, high temperature and light.

formula_sheet.name: Limiting factors
formula_sheet.expr: Blackman 1905; light saturates at 10 per cent of full sunlight; atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> 0.03 to 0.04 per cent; C<sub>4</sub> saturate at 360 µl L<sup>−1</sup>, C<sub>3</sub> beyond 450 µl L<sup>−1</sup>; C<sub>4</sub> higher temperature optimum; water stress closes stomata and wilts leaves
formula_sheet.note: Greenhouse tomatoes and bell pepper grown under CO<sub>2</sub> enrichment.

diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an oval with a double line for the envelope (label outer membrane and inner membrane). Inside, draw four or five stacks of flat discs and label one stack 'granum' and one disc 'thylakoid'; connect two grana with a thin membrane labelled 'stroma lamellae'. Shade the fluid around them and label 'stroma'. Point to the space inside one disc and label 'thylakoid lumen'. Add a small circle labelled 'ribosome' and a starch grain if you like. Marking points: envelope, grana, thylakoid, stroma lamellae, stroma; then one line saying membranes make ATP and NADPH, stroma fixes CO<sub>2</sub>.

diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes: x-axis wavelength of light in nm from 400 to 700, y-axis absorption (left) and rate of photosynthesis (right). Draw chlorophyll a as a curve with a tall peak near 430 nm (blue) and a second peak near 660 nm (red), with a deep trough in the green around 550 nm. Draw chlorophyll b with peaks slightly inside those (near 450 and 640 nm). Draw carotenoids with a single broad peak in the blue-violet region and nothing in the red. Superimpose a dashed action spectrum with the same two-peak shape. Label all curves and mark 'blue' and 'red' at the peaks and 'green (least absorbed)' at the trough. Write beneath: overlap of action spectrum with chlorophyll a shows chlorophyll a is the chief pigment.

diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a fan or funnel of many small circles labelled 'antenna pigment molecules' (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids) converging on one larger circle at the narrow end labelled 'reaction centre (chlorophyll a)'. Draw wavy arrows labelled 'light' hitting the antenna and short arrows inside showing energy transfer toward the centre. From the reaction centre draw one arrow labelled 'e<sup>−</sup> to primary acceptor'. Add a note: P700 in PS I, P680 in PS II.

diagrams.title: Z scheme of light reaction: non-cyclic photophosphorylation (NCERT Fig. 11.6)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical axis labelled 'redox potential' (negative at the top). At the bottom left write 'H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sup>+</sup> + ½O<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>' feeding into a box 'PS II (P680)'. Draw an arrow up from PS II labelled 'light (680 nm)' to 'primary acceptor'. Then a staircase going down through 'plastoquinone' and 'cytochromes' with 'ATP' written beside it, reaching a box 'PS I (P700)'. Draw another arrow up labelled 'light (700 nm)' to a second 'acceptor', then down through 'ferredoxin' to 'NADP reductase' and 'NADP<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → NADPH'. Two uphill arrows and two downhill runs give the Z. Marking points: P680, P700, both acceptors, ATP on the cytochrome chain, NADPH at the end, water splitting at PS II.

diagrams.title: Cyclic photophosphorylation flowchart (exemplar)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a box 'PS I (P700)' with an arrow labelled 'light beyond 680 nm' going up to 'electron acceptor'. From the acceptor draw an arrow down through a box labelled 'electron transport chain (cytochromes)' and back to PS I, closing the loop. Write 'ATP' beside the chain. Add three notes: only PS I involved, no water splitting or O<sub>2</sub>, no NADPH; site stroma lamellae.

diagrams.title: ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis in the thylakoid membrane (NCERT Fig. 11.7)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal band for the thylakoid membrane with 'lumen' below and 'stroma' above. In the membrane place, left to right, 'PS II' with 'H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sup>+</sup> + ½O<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>' releasing H<sup>+</sup> into the lumen; an 'H carrier / cytochrome complex' with an arrow carrying H<sup>+</sup> from stroma to lumen; 'PS I'; and on the stroma face 'NADP reductase' taking H<sup>+</sup> from the stroma to make NADPH. At the right draw ATP synthase: a cylinder in the membrane labelled 'F<sub>0</sub>' and a knob on the stroma side labelled 'F<sub>1</sub>', with H<sup>+</sup> flowing from lumen through F<sub>0</sub> into the stroma and 'ADP + Pi → ATP' at F<sub>1</sub>. Write 'high H<sup>+</sup>' in the lumen and 'low H<sup>+</sup>' in the stroma.
