diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle. At the top write 'CO<sub>2</sub>' entering at 'RuBP (5C)' with 'RuBisCO' beside it, the arrow leading to '2 × 3-PGA (3C)' and label this arm 'Carboxylation'. Continue clockwise: an arm labelled 'Reduction' with '2 ATP → 2 ADP' and '2 NADPH → 2 NADP<sup>+</sup>' feeding in, leading to 'triose phosphate'. Draw a side arrow out of the cycle from triose phosphate labelled 'sucrose / starch'. Continue the circle with an arm labelled 'Regeneration', '1 ATP → 1 ADP', back to RuBP. Beneath the circle write the balance sheet: In 6 CO<sub>2</sub>, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH; Out 1 glucose, 18 ADP, 12 NADP<sup>+</sup>.

diagrams.title: Kranz anatomy: T.S. of a C<sub>4</sub> leaf compared with a C<sub>3</sub> leaf (NCERT Fig. 11.9)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two leaf cross-sections side by side. For C<sub>3</sub>: upper epidermis, a layer of elongated palisade mesophyll, loose spongy mesophyll with air spaces, a vascular bundle with a thin ordinary sheath, lower epidermis with a stoma. For C<sub>4</sub>: upper and lower epidermis, mesophyll cells arranged in a ring, and a vascular bundle surrounded by a wreath of large, thick-walled bundle sheath cells packed with chloroplasts and no intercellular spaces; label 'bundle sheath cells (Kranz)', 'mesophyll cells', 'vascular bundle'. Write beneath: bundle sheath has RuBisCO and Calvin cycle; mesophyll has PEPcase; no photorespiration.

diagrams.title: Hatch and Slack (C<sub>4</sub>) pathway (NCERT Fig. 11.10)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two adjacent cells. Left cell labelled 'mesophyll cell': show 'CO<sub>2</sub>' entering, 'PEP (3C)' + CO<sub>2</sub> → 'OAA (4C)' with 'PEP carboxylase' on the arrow; OAA → 'C<sub>4</sub> acid (malate)'. Draw an arrow carrying the C<sub>4</sub> acid across the wall into the right cell labelled 'bundle sheath cell'. There show 'C<sub>4</sub> acid → CO<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>3</sub> acid (pyruvate)' and the CO<sub>2</sub> entering a small circle labelled 'Calvin cycle (RuBisCO)' with 'sugar' leaving. Draw an arrow bringing the C<sub>3</sub> acid back to the mesophyll cell where 'C<sub>3</sub> acid → PEP' with 'ATP' on the arrow. Two cells, four molecules, two enzymes named.

diagrams.title: Effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis (NCERT Fig. 11.11)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes: x-axis light intensity, y-axis rate of photosynthesis. Draw a curve rising linearly from the origin (mark this region A and label 'light limiting'), bending over (mark B), and becoming flat (mark C and D, label 'light saturation; CO<sub>2</sub> or temperature now limiting'). Write Blackman's law under the graph. If asked about CO<sub>2</sub> or temperature curves, draw the same shape with the C<sub>4</sub> curve saturating earlier and higher than the C<sub>3</sub> curve for CO<sub>2</sub>, and a bell-shaped curve with the C<sub>4</sub> optimum to the right for temperature.

ncert_questions.q: By looking at a plant externally can you tell whether a plant is C<sub>3</sub> or C<sub>4</sub>? Why and how?
ncert_questions.a: No. C3 and C4 plants cannot be distinguished by looking at them from outside, because the difference lies in the biochemistry (the first stable product, 3-PGA or OAA, and the presence of PEP carboxylase) and in the internal anatomy of the leaf, none of which is visible externally. Both kinds of plants have ordinary-looking green leaves, and many C4 plants (maize, sorghum, sugarcane) are grasses that look like C3 grasses such as wheat and rice. A transverse section of the leaf under the microscope, showing Kranz anatomy, or a biochemical test for the first product, is needed.

ncert_questions.q: By looking at which internal structure of a plant can you tell whether a plant is C<sub>3</sub> or C<sub>4</sub>? Explain.
ncert_questions.a: The internal structure of the leaf (a transverse section) tells us. C4 leaves show Kranz anatomy: the vascular bundles are surrounded by a wreath of large bundle sheath cells that have a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces, and the mesophyll cells are arranged around this sheath and are not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers. C3 leaves lack such a chloroplast-rich sheath; the bundle sheath, if present, has few or no chloroplasts, and the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma with intercellular spaces. In C4 plants the Calvin cycle runs only in the bundle sheath cells, which contain RuBisCO, while the mesophyll contains PEP carboxylase.

ncert_questions.q: Even though very few cells in a C<sub>4</sub> plant carry out the biosynthetic Calvin pathway, yet they are highly productive. Can you discuss why?
ncert_questions.a:
In a C4 plant only the bundle sheath cells carry out the Calvin cycle, but the plant is highly productive for these reasons:

  • The C4 pathway is a CO2 concentrating mechanism. Mesophyll cells fix CO2 into C4 acids using PEP carboxylase, which has a high affinity for CO2 and no oxygenase activity, and these acids are transported to the bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated there. So the bundle sheath cells receive a steady supply of CO2 at a high concentration, and RuBisCO works entirely as a carboxylase.
  • Because of the high CO2 around RuBisCO, photorespiration is absent; no fixed carbon is lost and no ATP is wasted on the photorespiratory pathway.
  • The thick, gas-impervious walls of the bundle sheath prevent the concentrated CO2 from leaking out.
  • C4 plants can keep photosynthesising with partly closed stomata, tolerate high temperatures and respond to high light intensities, so they photosynthesise at a high rate through the hottest, brightest part of the day when C3 plants slow down.

The whole leaf, in effect, feeds carbon to a few well-protected cells that run the Calvin cycle at maximum efficiency, so the biomass output is higher.

ncert_questions.q: RuBisCO is an enzyme that acts both as a carboxylase and oxygenase. Why do you think RuBisCO carries out more carboxylation in C<sub>4</sub> plants?
ncert_questions.a: The active site of RuBisCO binds both CO2 and O2, and which reaction occurs depends on their relative concentrations at the enzyme. In C4 plants RuBisCO is present only in the bundle sheath cells. The mesophyll cells fix CO2 into C4 acids (via PEP carboxylase, which does not react with O2), and these acids are transported to the bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated there, releasing CO2. This raises the intracellular CO2 concentration around RuBisCO far above the atmospheric level. With CO2 in large excess over O2, RuBisCO functions as a carboxylase and its oxygenase activity is minimised. Hence there is more carboxylation and negligible photorespiration in C4 plants.

ncert_questions.q: Suppose there were plants that have a high concentration of chlorophyll b, but lack chlorophyll a, would it carry out photosynthesis? Then why do plants have chlorophyll b and other accessory pigments?
ncert_questions.a:
No, such a plant would not carry out photosynthesis. Chlorophyll a is the reaction centre pigment of both photosystems (P700 in PS I, P680 in PS II) and is the only pigment that converts light energy into chemical energy by releasing an excited electron. Chlorophyll b and the other pigments cannot do this; they can only absorb light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a. Without chlorophyll a there is no reaction centre, no electron flow, and no ATP or NADPH.

Plants nevertheless have chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids because these accessory pigments (i) absorb light at wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and transfer that energy to chlorophyll a, so that a wider part of the spectrum is used and the efficiency of photosynthesis increases, and (ii) protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation by strong light.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the colour of a leaf kept in the dark frequently yellow, or pale green? Which pigment do you think is more stable?
ncert_questions.a: Light is needed for the synthesis of chlorophyll, and chlorophyll is continuously broken down in the leaf. In the dark, chlorophyll is not synthesised but its degradation continues, so the green colour fades. The carotenoids (xanthophylls and carotenes), which are yellow to orange, are more stable and do not need light for their maintenance, so they remain and the leaf appears yellow or pale green. Hence the carotenoids are more stable than chlorophyll. The same thing happens in autumn leaves and in etiolated seedlings grown in the dark.

ncert_questions.q: Look at leaves of the same plant on the shady side and compare them with the leaves on the sunny side. Or compare potted plants kept in the sunlight with those in the shade. Which of them has leaves that are darker green? Why?
ncert_questions.a: The leaves on the shady side (or of the plant kept in shade) are darker green. In shade, light is the limiting factor for photosynthesis. To capture as much of the available light as possible, shade leaves develop more chloroplasts per cell and a higher concentration of chlorophyll (and more chlorophyll b relative to chlorophyll a, which broadens the absorption range). Leaves in full sun receive far more light than they can use (light saturates at about 10 per cent of full sunlight), and very high light also causes some breakdown of chlorophyll, so sun leaves are lighter green.

ncert_questions.q: The figure shows the effect of light on the rate of photosynthesis. Based on the graph, answer the following: (a) At which point/s (A, B or C) in the curve is light a limiting factor? (b) What could be the limiting factor/s in region A? (c) What do C and D represent on the curve?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Light is a limiting factor in region A, where the rate rises linearly with light intensity (and to some extent up to B, where the curve begins to bend).

(b) In region A, light is the limiting factor: the rate depends directly on light intensity, and other factors (CO2, temperature, water) are present in adequate amounts.

(c) C is the point of light saturation: beyond it, increasing light intensity does not increase the rate, because some other factor, usually CO2 concentration (or temperature), has become limiting. D lies on the plateau and shows that the rate stays constant despite higher light; if light were increased far beyond this, chlorophyll breakdown would actually reduce the rate.

ncert_questions.q: Give a comparison between the C<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub> pathways.
ncert_questions.a:
Present as a table with these rows.

  • Primary CO2 acceptor: C3: RuBP (5C). C4: PEP (3C) in mesophyll (RuBP in bundle sheath).
  • First stable product: C3: 3-PGA (3C). C4: OAA (4C).
  • Enzyme of first fixation: C3: RuBisCO. C4: PEP carboxylase (RuBisCO later, in bundle sheath).
  • Cells involved: C3: mesophyll cells only. C4: mesophyll (C4 acid formation) and bundle sheath (Calvin cycle).
  • Leaf anatomy: C3: no Kranz anatomy. C4: Kranz anatomy.
  • Photorespiration: C3: present, high on hot bright days. C4: absent (CO2 concentrating mechanism).
  • ATP per glucose: C3: 18. C4: more (30), because PEP regeneration costs extra ATP.
  • CO2 saturation: C3: beyond 450 µl L−1. C4: about 360 µl L−1.
  • Temperature optimum and productivity: C3: lower optimum, lower biomass. C4: higher optimum, higher biomass.
  • Examples: C3: wheat, rice, most plants. C4: maize, sorghum, sugarcane.

ncert_questions.q: Give a comparison between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
ncert_questions.a:
• Photosystems involved: Cyclic: only PS I. Non-cyclic: both PS II and PS I.
  • Path of electrons: Cyclic: electron from P700 returns to PS I through the electron transport chain. Non-cyclic: electrons flow from water through PS II, cytochromes and PS I to NADP+ and do not return.
  • Splitting of water and O2 evolution: Cyclic: no. Non-cyclic: yes.
  • Products: Cyclic: ATP only. Non-cyclic: ATP and NADPH (and O2).
  • Site: Cyclic: stroma lamellae (which lack PS II and NADP reductase). Non-cyclic: grana lamellae.
  • Light conditions: Cyclic: occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available. Non-cyclic: needs both 680 nm and 700 nm light.

ncert_questions.q: Give a comparison between the anatomy of the leaf in C<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub> plants.
ncert_questions.a:
• Bundle sheath: C3: bundle sheath cells, if present, are small and contain few or no chloroplasts. C4: large bundle sheath cells in one or several layers around the vascular bundle, with a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces (Kranz anatomy).
  • Mesophyll: C3: differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma with intercellular spaces. C4: undifferentiated mesophyll cells arranged around the bundle sheath.
  • Chloroplast types: C3: one kind of chloroplast in the mesophyll. C4: dimorphic, mesophyll chloroplasts with grana, bundle sheath chloroplasts often with poorly developed grana.
  • Enzyme distribution: C3: RuBisCO in mesophyll. C4: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll, RuBisCO in bundle sheath; the Calvin cycle runs only in the bundle sheath.

ncert_questions.q: Explain how ATP synthesis during the light reaction is a chemiosmotic phenomenon.
ncert_questions.a: ATP synthesis is called chemiosmotic because it is driven by a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, not by a direct chemical intermediate. The gradient develops in three ways: (i) water is split on the inner side of the membrane, so its protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen; (ii) the primary acceptor of PS II passes its electron to an H carrier, which picks up a proton from the stroma and releases it into the lumen as the electron moves to the next carrier on the inner side; (iii) NADP reductase on the stroma side uses protons from the stroma to make NADPH. Protons therefore accumulate in the lumen and are depleted in the stroma. The gradient is released only through the F0 channel of ATP synthase; the flow of protons through F0 causes a conformational change in the F1 part facing the stroma, which catalyses ADP + Pi → ATP. The membrane, the proton pump, the gradient and ATP synthase are the four requirements.

ncert_questions.q: Why is RuBisCO the most abundant enzyme in the world?
ncert_questions.a: RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is present in the chloroplasts of every photosynthetic plant, alga and cyanobacterium on earth, because all of them run the Calvin cycle, and RuBisCO catalyses its first and rate-limiting step, the carboxylation of RuBP. It is a slow and inefficient enzyme with a low turnover, and its active site also binds O2, so a cell must make it in very large quantities (it can be up to half the soluble protein of a leaf) to fix enough CO2. The enormous number of photosynthetic cells multiplied by the large amount in each makes RuBisCO the most abundant protein in the biosphere.

ncert_questions.q: What is Kranz anatomy? In which plants is it found? What advantage does it give over C<sub>3</sub> plants?
ncert_questions.a: Kranz anatomy (Kranz means wreath) is the leaf anatomy in which large bundle sheath cells, rich in chloroplasts, with thick walls impervious to gases and no intercellular spaces, form one or more layers around each vascular bundle, with the mesophyll cells arranged around the sheath. It is found in C4 plants such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane. Its advantage is that it separates the two stages of the C4 pathway: CO2 is fixed by PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll and released from C4 acids in the sealed bundle sheath, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle operate at a high CO2 concentration. This suppresses photorespiration, lets the plant work at high temperature and light and with partly closed stomata, and gives higher productivity than C3 plants.

pyq.q: Which metal ion is a constituent of chlorophyll?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The porphyrin ring of chlorophyll has a magnesium ion at its centre. Iron is in cytochromes, and copper in plastocyanin.

pyq.q: Which pigment acts directly to convert light energy into chemical energy?
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Only chlorophyll a forms the reaction centre (P680, P700) and releases an excited electron. The others are accessory pigments that pass energy to it.

pyq.q: Which range of wavelength (in nm) is called photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: PAR is the visible band, about 400 to 700 nm, that plants use for photosynthesis.

pyq.q: During the light reaction in photosynthesis, the following are formed:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The light reaction makes ATP, NADPH (the hydrogen donor for CO<sub>2</sub> reduction) and O<sub>2</sub> from water splitting. Sugar is made in the dark reaction.

pyq.q: The correct sequence of flow of electrons in the light reaction is:
options: PS II, plastoquinone, cytochromes, PS I, ferredoxin
PS I, plastoquinone, cytochromes, PS II, ferredoxin
PS I, plastoquinone, cytochromes, PS II, ferredoxin
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: In the Z scheme PS II acts first; its electron goes through plastoquinone and the cytochrome chain to PS I, and then via ferredoxin to NADP<sup>+</sup>.

pyq.q: The enzyme that is not found in a C<sub>3</sub> plant is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: PEP carboxylase fixes CO<sub>2</sub> into OAA in the mesophyll of C<sub>4</sub> plants only. RuBisCO, NADP reductase and ATP synthase are present in all photosynthetic plants.

pyq.q: When CO<sub>2</sub> is added to PEP, the first stable product synthesised is:
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: PEP (3C) + CO<sub>2</sub> gives the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid, the first stable product of the C<sub>4</sub> pathway. Phosphoglycerate is the first product of the C<sub>3</sub> pathway.

pyq.q: Splitting of water is associated with:
options: Inner surface of the thylakoid membrane
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The water-splitting complex is linked to PS II, which is located on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane; the protons are released into the lumen but the complex itself sits on the membrane surface.

pyq.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation results in the formation of:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In cyclic flow the electron from P700 returns to PS I; no water is split, so no O<sub>2</sub> and no NADPH; only ATP is formed along the chain.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): C<sub>4</sub> plants do not show photorespiration. Reason (R): In C<sub>4</sub> plants, the C<sub>4</sub> acid is decarboxylated in the bundle sheath cells, raising the CO<sub>2</sub> concentration around RuBisCO.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The CO<sub>2</sub> concentrating mechanism keeps RuBisCO working as a carboxylase, so its oxygenase activity, and hence photorespiration, is suppressed. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The dark reaction of photosynthesis occurs only at night. Reason (R): The dark reaction does not directly depend on light but uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The dark reaction runs mainly in daylight, when ATP and NADPH are available; it is called dark only because it does not need light directly. So A is false and R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Cyclic photophosphorylation is thought to occur in the stroma lamellae. Reason (R): The stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Without PS II there is no water splitting and without NADP reductase no NADPH can be made, so only the cyclic route using PS I is possible in the stroma lamellae. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A plant with chlorophyll b but no chlorophyll a cannot carry out photosynthesis. Reason (R): Chlorophyll b absorbs light in the blue and red regions of the spectrum.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A is true because chlorophyll a alone forms the reaction centre. R is also true (chlorophyll b absorbs in blue and red) but it does not explain why the plant fails; the reason is the absence of a reaction centre.

pyq.q: Write the equation for the splitting of water in photosynthesis. Where does it take place, and what happens to each product?
pyq.answer: 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−. It takes place at the water-splitting complex associated with PS II, on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane. The electrons replace those lost by P680, the protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen and build the proton gradient for ATP synthesis, and the O2 is released as a by-product.

pyq.q: Differentiate between absorption spectrum and action spectrum. What conclusion is drawn from their overlap?
pyq.answer: An absorption spectrum is a graph of the amount of light absorbed by a pigment against wavelength. An action spectrum is a graph of the rate of photosynthesis against wavelength. Because the action spectrum of photosynthesis closely overlaps the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a (peaks in blue and red, trough in green), chlorophyll a is concluded to be the chief pigment of photosynthesis; the small mismatch shows that accessory pigments also contribute.

pyq.q: Name the primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor and the first stable product in (a) C<sub>3</sub> plants and (b) C<sub>4</sub> plants, with the number of carbon atoms in each.
pyq.answer: (a) C3 plants: acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, RuBP (5 carbons); first stable product 3-phosphoglyceric acid, 3-PGA (3 carbons). (b) C4 plants: acceptor phosphoenol pyruvate, PEP (3 carbons); first stable product oxaloacetic acid, OAA (4 carbons).

pyq.q: How many molecules of ATP and NADPH are required to fix one molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> in the Calvin cycle, and to make one molecule of glucose? Where does this take place?
pyq.answer: Per CO2: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH (2 ATP and 2 NADPH in reduction, 1 ATP in regeneration of RuBP). Per glucose (6 CO2, six turns): 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast.

pyq.q: State two conditions under which cyclic photophosphorylation takes place in a chloroplast.
pyq.answer: (i) When only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available, since such light excites P700 of PS I but not P680 of PS II. (ii) In the stroma lamellae, which have PS I but lack PS II and NADP reductase, so the non-cyclic route cannot operate there. (Also acceptable: when the cell needs extra ATP relative to NADPH for the Calvin cycle.)

pyq.q: Describe the experiments of Engelmann and van Niel and state what each established.
pyq.answer:
Engelmann used a prism to split light into its spectral components and illuminated a filament of the green alga Cladophora placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. The bacteria, which move towards oxygen, accumulated mainly in the blue and red regions of the split spectrum, where the alga was releasing the most oxygen. This gave the first action spectrum of photosynthesis and showed that blue and red light are most effective, matching the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll.

Van Niel studied purple and green sulphur bacteria, which use H2S as the hydrogen donor and release sulphur instead of oxygen. He proposed that photosynthesis is essentially a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from a suitable oxidisable compound reduces CO2 to carbohydrate, 2H2A + CO2 → 2A + CH2O + H2O, and that in green plants water is the hydrogen donor, so the O2 evolved comes from water and not from CO2. This was later proved with radioisotopes.

pyq.q: Explain the three stages of the Calvin cycle, mentioning the enzyme of the first stage and the ATP and NADPH used in each.
pyq.answer:
Carboxylation: CO2 is fixed onto the 5-carbon acceptor RuBP by the enzyme RuBP carboxylase (RuBisCO), giving an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid. No ATP or NADPH is used. This is the most crucial step.

Reduction: 3-PGA is phosphorylated using ATP and reduced using NADPH to triose phosphate, from which glucose is formed. 2 ATP and 2 NADPH are used per CO2 fixed. Six turns of the cycle (six CO2) are needed to remove one glucose.

Regeneration: The acceptor RuBP is re-formed from triose phosphates so that the cycle can continue; this uses 1 ATP per CO2 for the phosphorylation that forms RuBP. Total per CO2: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH; per glucose: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

pyq.q: What is photorespiration? Under what conditions does it occur, and why is it considered a wasteful process?
pyq.answer:
Photorespiration is the light-dependent process in C3 plants in which RuBisCO binds O2 instead of CO2, so that RuBP is converted to one molecule of phosphoglycerate (3C) and one of phosphoglycolate (2C) instead of two molecules of 3-PGA.

It occurs when the concentration of O2 is high relative to CO2 at the enzyme: on hot, bright days when stomata partly close, internal CO2 falls and O2 from the light reaction builds up; high temperature also lowers RuBisCO's relative affinity for CO2.

It is wasteful because in the photorespiratory pathway there is no synthesis of sugar, ATP or NADPH; instead fixed carbon is lost as CO2 and ATP is consumed. C4 plants avoid it by concentrating CO2 in the bundle sheath cells.

pyq.q: State Blackman's law of limiting factors and explain it with the help of a graph of light intensity against the rate of photosynthesis.
pyq.answer:
Blackman's law (1905): if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, then its rate will be determined by the factor which is nearest to its minimal value; it is the factor which directly affects the process if its quantity is changed.

Draw the graph with light intensity on the x-axis and rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis. At low intensities the curve rises linearly: light is the limiting factor, and increasing it increases the rate. The curve then bends and becomes flat at the light-saturation point (about 10 per cent of full sunlight). Beyond it, more light does not raise the rate because another factor, usually CO2 concentration or temperature, is now nearest its minimum and has become limiting. If CO2 is then increased, the plateau rises to a new level. Thus at any moment a single factor sets the rate.

pyq.q: Distinguish between the role of the mesophyll cells and the bundle sheath cells in the C<sub>4</sub> pathway. Which enzymes does each contain?
pyq.answer:
Mesophyll cells: carry out the primary fixation of CO2. The 3-carbon acceptor PEP combines with CO2 to form 4-carbon OAA, catalysed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase). OAA is converted to other C4 acids (malate, aspartate) that are exported to the bundle sheath. The mesophyll cells also regenerate PEP from the returning 3-carbon acid, using ATP. They contain PEPcase but lack RuBisCO.

Bundle sheath cells: receive the C4 acids and decarboxylate them, releasing CO2 and a 3-carbon acid (pyruvate). The released CO2 enters the Calvin cycle, which runs only here, and sugar is made. They are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase. Their thick gas-impervious walls keep the CO2 concentration high, so RuBisCO works as a carboxylase and photorespiration is avoided.

pyq.q: Describe, with a labelled diagram, the Z scheme of electron transport in the light reaction of photosynthesis. Name the products formed.
pyq.answer:
Draw the Z scheme (redox potential on the vertical axis; PS II bottom left, PS I to the right; two uphill light arrows, two downhill electron runs; water splitting at PS II, NADPH at the end, ATP on the cytochrome chain). Then describe:

  1. In PS II the reaction centre chlorophyll a, P680, absorbs 680 nm red light and its excited electron is taken up by a primary electron acceptor.
  2. The electron passes from the acceptor to an electron transport system of cytochromes (via plastoquinone), moving downhill in terms of redox potential; the energy released is used to make ATP by chemiosmosis (photophosphorylation).
  3. The electron reaches the pigments of PS I, replacing the electron lost by P700.
  4. P700 absorbs 700 nm red light, is excited and transfers its electron to another acceptor of higher redox potential.
  5. From this acceptor the electron moves downhill through ferredoxin to NADP+, which the enzyme NADP reductase reduces to NADPH + H+.
  6. The electron deficit in PS II is made up by the splitting of water: 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−, on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane; O2 is released.

Because the electrons flow in one direction from water to NADP+ and never return, the scheme is called non-cyclic photophosphorylation; the shape of the pathway on a redox scale gives it the name Z scheme. Products: ATP, NADPH and O2.

pyq.q: Explain the C<sub>4</sub> pathway of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation with a diagram. Mention the special anatomical feature of C<sub>4</sub> leaves and list the advantages C<sub>4</sub> plants have over C<sub>3</sub> plants.
pyq.answer:
Anatomy. C4 plants (maize, sorghum, sugarcane) show Kranz anatomy: the vascular bundles are surrounded by large bundle sheath cells with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces, with the mesophyll cells arranged around them.

Pathway (Hatch and Slack pathway). Draw a mesophyll cell and a bundle sheath cell side by side.

  1. In the mesophyll cell the 3-carbon acceptor phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) fixes CO2 to form the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (OAA), catalysed by PEP carboxylase. Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO.
  2. OAA is converted to other 4-carbon acids (malic or aspartic acid) that are transported to the bundle sheath cells.
  3. In the bundle sheath cells the C4 acid is decarboxylated, releasing CO2 and a 3-carbon acid (pyruvate).
  4. The released CO2 enters the Calvin cycle, which runs in the bundle sheath cells (rich in RuBisCO), and sugar is formed.
  5. The 3-carbon acid returns to the mesophyll cell and is converted back to PEP using ATP, completing the cycle.

Advantages. (i) The pathway is a CO2 concentrating mechanism, so RuBisCO works as a carboxylase and photorespiration is absent. (ii) C4 plants tolerate higher temperatures and have a higher temperature optimum. (iii) They respond to high light intensities. (iv) They can photosynthesise with partly closed stomata, saving water. (v) They show greater productivity of biomass and saturate at a lower CO2 concentration (about 360 µl L−1).

pyq.q: Describe the chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis in chloroplasts. How is the proton gradient created and how is it used?
pyq.answer:
According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis (Peter Mitchell), ATP synthesis in the chloroplast is linked to a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, with protons accumulating inside the thylakoid lumen. Draw the thylakoid membrane with lumen below and stroma above, showing PS II, the H carrier, PS I, NADP reductase and ATP synthase (F0 in the membrane, F1 facing the stroma).

Creation of the gradient (three events):

  1. Splitting of water takes place on the inner side of the membrane, so the protons produced accumulate in the lumen.
  2. The primary electron acceptor of PS II, on the outer side of the membrane, transfers its electron to an H carrier; this molecule removes a proton from the stroma while carrying the electron and releases the proton into the lumen when it hands the electron to the next carrier on the inner side. Protons are thus pumped from stroma to lumen.
  3. NADP reductase, on the stroma side of the membrane, uses protons from the stroma to reduce NADP+ to NADPH + H+, further lowering the proton concentration in the stroma.

The result is a high proton concentration (low pH) in the lumen and a low proton concentration in the stroma.

Use of the gradient. The gradient is broken down only by movement of protons through the transmembrane channel F0 of the enzyme ATP synthase, by facilitated diffusion. The energy released as the protons pass through F0 produces a conformational change in the F1 portion, which protrudes into the stroma, and F1 then synthesises ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. The requirements are therefore a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase. The ATP and NADPH formed are used in the stroma to fix CO2.

pyq.q: Explain how light intensity, CO<sub>2</sub> concentration, temperature and water affect the rate of photosynthesis. Why is CO<sub>2</sub> considered the major limiting factor?
pyq.answer:
Light. At low intensities the rate is directly proportional to light intensity (linear part of the curve). Light saturation occurs at about 10 per cent of full sunlight; beyond that, other factors limit the rate, so light is rarely limiting in nature except in shade and dense forests. Very high light causes breakdown of chlorophyll and reduces the rate.

CO2. The atmosphere contains only 0.03 to 0.04 per cent CO2. Increasing it up to about 0.05 per cent raises the rate; beyond that it is damaging over long periods. At low light neither C3 nor C4 plants respond much to extra CO2; at high light both do. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µl L−1, while C3 plants continue to respond and saturate only beyond 450 µl L−1. This is exploited in greenhouses, where tomatoes and bell pepper are grown in CO2-enriched air for higher yield.

Temperature. The dark reactions are enzymatic and therefore strongly temperature dependent; the light reactions are affected much less. C4 plants have a higher temperature optimum and respond to higher temperatures; C3 plants have a much lower optimum. Tropical plants have higher optima than temperate plants.

Water. Water stress closes the stomata, reducing CO2 entry, and makes leaves wilt, reducing surface area and metabolic activity; so its effect is mostly indirect.

Why CO2 is the major limiting factor. Because its atmospheric concentration is far below the level at which photosynthesis saturates (especially for C3 plants), and light is usually above saturation in the open, CO2 is the factor nearest its minimum value, and by Blackman's law it sets the rate.

pyq.q:
A student placed a filament of the green alga Cladophora in a drop of water containing motile aerobic bacteria on a slide, and illuminated it with light that had been passed through a prism so that the filament received violet at one end and red at the other. After some minutes the bacteria were seen clustered mainly around the parts of the filament receiving blue and red light, with very few near the part receiving green light.
(i) Which scientist first performed this experiment, and what was it designed to find?
(ii) Why did the bacteria gather in the blue and red regions?
(iii) Name the type of spectrum obtained and state what it shows when compared with the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a.
(iv) Give one reason why green light was least effective.
pyq.answer:
(i) T. W. Engelmann; it was designed to find which wavelengths of light are most effective in photosynthesis. (1 mark)

(ii) The alga released the most oxygen in the blue and red regions, because chlorophyll absorbs these wavelengths most; the aerobic bacteria moved towards the oxygen and accumulated there. (1 mark)

(iii) An action spectrum of photosynthesis. Its peaks in blue and red coincide with the peaks of the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a, showing that chlorophyll a is the chief pigment driving photosynthesis. (1 mark)

(iv) Green light is largely reflected or transmitted by the leaf rather than absorbed by chlorophyll, so it drives little photosynthesis (and little O2 release). (1 mark)

pyq.q:
A farmer grows maize in one field and wheat in an adjoining field during a hot, bright summer. The maize continues to grow rapidly through the afternoon, while the wheat shows a marked drop in growth. A leaf section of the maize shows large chloroplast-rich cells around each vascular bundle, which the wheat section lacks. Meanwhile, in his greenhouse, the farmer has started enriching the air with CO2 for his tomato crop and finds the yield rises.
(i) Which of the two crops is a C4 plant? Name the anatomical feature seen in its leaf.
(ii) Why does the wheat slow down in the hot bright afternoon while the maize does not?
(iii) In which cells of the maize leaf does the Calvin cycle occur, and which enzyme fixes CO2 in its mesophyll cells?
(iv) Why does CO2 enrichment raise tomato yield, and would it help maize as much?
pyq.answer:
(i) Maize is the C4 plant. The feature is Kranz anatomy, with large bundle sheath cells full of chloroplasts around the vascular bundles. (1 mark)

(ii) In hot bright conditions wheat (a C3 plant) partly closes its stomata; internal CO2 falls and O2 rises, so RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase and photorespiration wastes fixed carbon and ATP. Maize concentrates CO2 in its bundle sheath cells through the C4 pathway, so photorespiration is absent, and it also has a higher temperature optimum and responds to high light. (1 mark)

(iii) The Calvin cycle occurs in the bundle sheath cells. In the mesophyll cells CO2 is fixed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase) onto PEP to form OAA. (1 mark)

(iv) Tomato is a C3 plant, and atmospheric CO2 (0.03 to 0.04 per cent) is limiting for C3 photosynthesis, which saturates only beyond 450 µl L−1; raising CO2 therefore raises the rate and yield. Maize, being C4, saturates at about 360 µl L−1, close to present levels, so enrichment would help it much less. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.q: Which light range is least effective in photosynthesis?
practice_mcq.explanation: Green light is mostly reflected by chlorophyll, which is why leaves look green; blue and red are absorbed most.

practice_mcq.q: Dark reaction in photosynthesis is called so because
options: it can occur only in the dark
it does not directly depend on light energy
it occurs more rapidly at night
practice_mcq.explanation: The biosynthetic phase does not need light directly but uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction, so it actually runs in daylight.

practice_mcq.q: PEP is the primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor in
practice_mcq.explanation: Phosphoenol pyruvate accepts CO<sub>2</sub> in the mesophyll cells of C<sub>4</sub> plants to form OAA; C<sub>3</sub> plants use RuBP.

practice_mcq.q: The energy required for ATP synthesis in the thylakoid comes from
options: the proton gradient across the membrane
practice_mcq.explanation: By the chemiosmotic hypothesis, protons accumulated in the lumen flow through F<sub>0</sub> of ATP synthase and the released energy drives ATP formation at F<sub>1</sub>.

practice_mcq.q: The reaction centre of photosystem I is
practice_mcq.explanation: PS I has a chlorophyll a reaction centre with an absorption peak at 700 nm (P700); PS II has P680.

practice_mcq.q: The first stable product of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation in the Calvin cycle is
practice_mcq.explanation: RuBP + CO<sub>2</sub> gives an unstable 6-carbon compound that splits into two molecules of 3-PGA, the first stable product.
Chemosynthetic bacteria oxidise inorganic compounds such as ammonia, nitrite or sulphur to obtain energy, unlike photosynthetic organisms that use light.

practice_mcq.q: The number of ATP and NADPH molecules required to make one molecule of glucose in the Calvin cycle is
practice_mcq.explanation: Each CO<sub>2</sub> needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH; six turns for one glucose give 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

practice_mcq.q: In the chromatogram of a leaf extract, chlorophyll b appears
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives chlorophyll a as bright or blue-green, chlorophyll b as yellow-green, xanthophylls as yellow and carotenoids as yellow to yellow-orange.

practice_mcq.q: Light saturation for photosynthesis in most plants occurs at about
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states that light saturation occurs at 10 per cent of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting in nature except under shade.

practice_mcq.q: The products of the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO are
options: one molecule of phosphoglycerate and one of phosphoglycolate
one molecule of pyruvate and one of PEP
practice_mcq.explanation: When RuBP reacts with O<sub>2</sub>, a 3-carbon phosphoglycerate and a 2-carbon phosphoglycolate are formed, starting photorespiration.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a C<sub>4</sub> plant?
practice_mcq.explanation: Sugarcane, maize and sorghum are the C<sub>4</sub> examples in NCERT; wheat, rice and potato are C<sub>3</sub>.

practice_mcq.q: The F<sub>1</sub> portion of the ATP synthase of a chloroplast
options: is embedded in the thylakoid membrane and forms a proton channel
protrudes on the stroma side and undergoes a conformational change to make ATP
practice_mcq.explanation: F<sub>0</sub> is the transmembrane proton channel; F<sub>1</sub> faces the stroma and synthesises ATP when protons flow through F<sub>0</sub>.

practice_mcq.q: The scientist who showed that the O<sub>2</sub> evolved in photosynthesis comes from water, using sulphur bacteria, was
practice_mcq.explanation: Cornelius van Niel worked with purple and green sulphur bacteria, which release sulphur from H<sub>2</sub>S, and inferred that plants release O<sub>2</sub> from H<sub>2</sub>O.

practice_mcq.q: C<sub>4</sub> plants show CO<sub>2</sub> saturation at about
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: C<sub>4</sub> plants saturate at about 360 µl L<sup>−1</sup>, while C<sub>3</sub> plants keep responding and saturate only beyond 450 µl L<sup>−1</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: Mesophyll cells of a C<sub>4</sub> plant lack
practice_mcq.explanation: In C<sub>4</sub> plants RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle are confined to the bundle sheath cells; the mesophyll has PEPcase and PEP.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about photorespiration is correct?
options: It synthesises sugar in the peroxisome
It releases CO<sub>2</sub> with the utilisation of ATP
It occurs in C<sub>4</sub> plants but not in C<sub>3</sub> plants
practice_mcq.explanation: Photorespiration makes no sugar, ATP or NADPH; it loses CO<sub>2</sub> and consumes ATP, and it is absent in C<sub>4</sub> plants.

practice_mcq.q: The stroma lamellae differ from the grana lamellae in lacking
practice_mcq.explanation: Stroma lamellae have PS I but lack PS II and NADP reductase, which is why only cyclic photophosphorylation is possible there.

common_mistakes: Writing the overall equation with 6H<sub>2</sub>O on the left. At this level use 12H<sub>2</sub>O on the left and 6H<sub>2</sub>O on the right, and say that the O<sub>2</sub> comes from water; the examiner is checking that point.
Saying PS I acts first because it is numbered one. The photosystems are numbered by order of discovery; PS II (P680) is excited first and passes electrons to PS I (P700).
Placing the proton accumulation in the stroma. In chloroplasts protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen and the stroma loses protons; F<sub>1</sub> of ATP synthase faces the stroma.

Attaching NADPH to the regeneration stage of the Calvin cycle. NADPH (2 per CO<sub>2</sub>) is used only in reduction; regeneration uses 1 ATP. Per glucose the totals are 18 ATP and 12 NADPH, not 12 and 18.
Calling the dark reaction a night-time process. It does not need light directly but needs the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction, so it runs in daylight; the better name is biosynthetic phase.
Describing photorespiration as a form of respiration that yields energy. It consumes O<sub>2</sub> and ATP, releases CO<sub>2</sub> and makes no sugar, ATP or NADPH; it is a loss.

Mixing up the C<sub>4</sub> cells: RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle are in the bundle sheath, PEP carboxylase and OAA formation in the mesophyll. Writing them the other way round loses the whole 5-mark answer.

Confusing Engelmann (prism, Cladophora, aerobic bacteria, action spectrum) with van Niel (sulphur bacteria, O<sub>2</sub> from water), and Priestley (plants restore air) with Ingenhousz (light and green parts needed).

Drawing the Z scheme without the axis or the two uphill arrows. A flat chain of boxes is not a Z scheme; show redox potential vertically, two light-driven rises and two downhill runs, with ATP on the cytochrome chain and NADPH at the end.
strategy:
Divide the chapter into three blocks and give each a study session. Block one is the setup: definition and equation, the five early experiments, the chloroplast and its division of labour, and the pigments with the absorption and action spectra. This block is mostly 1-mark and 2-mark material, so make a one-page table of names, findings, pigment colours and wavelengths and test yourself on it twice.

Block two is the light reaction, and it is where the 5-mark questions come from. Draw the Z scheme from memory until you can place P680, P700, both acceptors, the cytochrome chain with ATP, ferredoxin, NADP reductase and water splitting without looking. Then write the cyclic versus non-cyclic table (six rows) and the three ways the proton gradient forms, and draw ATP synthase with F0 in the membrane and F1 in the stroma. Every one of these has been a 3-mark or 5-mark question.

Block three is carbon fixation: the Calvin cycle with its three stages and the 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2 bookkeeping, the C4 pathway with the two cells and four molecules, Kranz anatomy, photorespiration and why C4 plants avoid it, then the four factors with Blackman's law and the light graph. The NCERT exercise 9 comparisons (C3 versus C4, cyclic versus non-cyclic, leaf anatomy) should be written out as tables and memorised as tables.

In the exam, always draw the diagram when a mechanism is asked, label it in NCERT words, and then write the steps as a numbered list. Biology marking rewards the correct term in the correct place: write RuBisCO not 'the enzyme', bundle sheath cells not 'those cells', thylakoid lumen not 'inside'. Keep the numbers ready: 400 to 700 nm, 680 and 700 nm, 10 per cent of sunlight, 0.03 to 0.04 per cent CO2, 360 and 450 µl L−1, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
